findings.title: Cascade: Revolt authenticate() closes its own session via context manager, breaking all subsequent API calls
findings.why_it_matters: The entire Revolt plugin is non-functional after authentication. Every subsequent API call (send_message, send_typing, get_user, get_channel, handle_events) will fail because the aiohttp session is closed.
evidence: Trigger: RevoltAdapter.connect() calls self._client.authenticate()
Step 1: authenticate() creates `async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:` (line 55)
Step 2: Inside the context manager, it stores `self._session = session` (line 56)
Step 3: authenticate() returns True, exiting the `async with` block
Step 4: The context manager calls session.close() on exit — self._session now references a CLOSED session
Step 5: Any subsequent call (send_message at line 100, handle_events at line 216) uses self._session which is closed
Outcome: aiohttp raises RuntimeError or ClientConnectionError on every API call after auth succeeds
The bug is deterministic — it happens on every successful authentication
findings.suggested_fix: Move the aiohttp.ClientSession creation outside the context manager. Create the session in authenticate() without `async with`, store it, and only close it in the close() method. Or restructure to use the session as a persistent resource created once and reused.

findings.title: Cascade: Zeus chip_in crashes with RuntimeError when called from any async context (including aiohttp handlers)
findings.why_it_matters: handle_chip_in() calls asyncio.run() which creates a new event loop. If this tool is invoked from within an existing event loop — which is the normal case when Hermes gateway runs on asyncio — it raises RuntimeError: 'This event loop is already running'. The chip-in feature is completely broken in production.
evidence: Trigger: Zeus calls the chip_in tool (normal operation after responding to a user message)
Step 1: handle_chip_in() is a synchronous function (line 96)
Step 2: It defines an async _run() function and calls asyncio.run(_run()) at line 120
Step 3: asyncio.run() attempts to create a new event loop
Step 4: If called from within an existing event loop (Hermes gateway runs on asyncio), Python raises RuntimeError
Outcome: chip_in always crashes in production with RuntimeError, returning no chip-ins
Note: The same pattern exists in routing.py's _call_profile (line 111) but it uses blocking subprocess.run which works from sync context — only chip_in uses asyncio.run()
findings.suggested_fix: Replace asyncio.run() with a pattern that detects an existing event loop. Use asyncio.get_event_loop().run_until_complete() for sync contexts, or check with asyncio.get_running_loop() and use loop.run_until_complete(). Alternatively, make handle_chip_in async and use await asyncio.gather() directly.

findings.title: Cascade: Revolt WebSocket reconnects permanently stop after 5 transient errors, even after network recovers
findings.why_it_matters: The retry counter in RevoltErrorHandler is never reset on successful reconnection. After any 5 transient errors (network blip, Revolt server restart, rate limit), the handler returns -1 forever. The bot becomes permanently disconnected until the entire Hermes process is restarted.
evidence: Trigger: Revolt WebSocket experiences 5 transient errors (e.g., network interruption, server restart)
Step 1: Each error calls error_handler.get_backoff() in adapter._run_websocket() (line 211)
Step 2: get_backoff() increments _retry_count (line 40) and returns the delay
Step 3: After 5 errors, _retry_count == 5, get_backoff() returns -1 (line 33-37)
Step 4: adapter._run_websocket() sleeps for -1 seconds (line 213: await asyncio.sleep(-1) — returns immediately)
Step 5: Loop continues, get_backoff() keeps returning -1, reconnect attempts happen with zero delay
Step 6: Even if the WebSocket connects successfully, _error_handler.reset() is NEVER called
Outcome: Permanent disconnection. The bot never recovers even after the network is fully restored
The reset() method exists (line 46-49) but is never called anywhere in the codebase
findings.suggested_fix: Call self._error_handler.reset() in adapter._run_websocket() after a successful handle_events() connection (after line 188, before the next iteration). Also add a minimum sleep delay when get_backoff() returns -1 to prevent tight reconnect loops.

findings.title: Cascade: Supervisor health monitor creates infinite restart loop for always-on profiles that crash on startup
findings.why_it_matters: If an always-on profile crashes immediately after starting (bad config, missing dependency, OOM), the health monitor detects it as crashed and restarts it. The profile crashes again immediately. This creates a tight restart loop that consumes CPU, fills logs, and may trigger rate limits or file descriptor exhaustion.
evidence: Trigger: An always-on profile (e.g., zeus, metis) crashes within 30 seconds of starting
Step 1: HealthMonitor._run() checks all profiles every 30 seconds (line 67)
Step 2: _check_all() finds the profile status is 'crashed' (line 72)
Step 3: run_mode is 'always-on', so _on_crash() is called (line 76)
Step 4: _default_restart() calls lifecycle.start_profile() (line 36)
Step 5: Profile starts, crashes again within seconds
Step 6: Next 30-second check detects crash again, restarts again
Step 7: No cooldown, no crash counter, no exponential backoff — infinite loop
Outcome: CPU waste, log flooding, potential file descriptor exhaustion from repeated subprocess spawns
The lifecycle.start_profile() writes a new PID file each time, orphaning old PID files if the process dies before cleanup
findings.suggested_fix: Add a crash counter and cooldown period to HealthMonitor. Track crash timestamps per profile. If a profile crashes N times within M minutes, stop attempting restarts and log a fatal error. Use exponential backoff between restart attempts.

findings.title: Race condition: Supervisor start_profile has TOCTOU gap allowing duplicate profile processes
findings.why_it_matters: Two concurrent requests to start the same profile can both pass the _read_pid() check and launch duplicate processes. This causes resource waste, conflicting database access, and unpredictable behavior since two instances of the same profile run simultaneously.
evidence: Trigger: Two concurrent calls to start_profile('zeus') — e.g., Zeus tool call + auto-start + manual API call
Step 1: Thread A calls _read_pid('zeus') at line 102 — returns None (no PID file)
Step 2: Thread B calls _read_pid('zeus') at line 102 — also returns None (PID file not yet written)
Step 3: Thread A calls subprocess.Popen() at line 107 — starts process A
Step 4: Thread B calls subprocess.Popen() at line 107 — starts process B
Step 5: Thread A writes PID file for process A at line 120
Step 6: Thread B writes PID file for process B at line 120 — overwrites A's PID
Outcome: Two zeus processes running. Only B's PID is tracked. A is orphaned and unmanageable.
The _init_lock in supervisor/__init__.py only protects plugin registration, not start_profile calls
The tool handler _handle_start_profile (line 94) has no locking either
findings.suggested_fix: Add a threading.Lock (or file-based lock for cross-process safety) around the check-then-start sequence in start_profile. Use fcntl.flock on the PID file for cross-process atomicity.

findings.title: Abuse case: Dashboard auth allows anyone to set the admin password via first-login race
findings.why_it_matters: The first login attempt creates the password hash. If the dashboard is exposed to any network (even localhost), an attacker who hits the login endpoint first sets the password. The legitimate user is then locked out permanently.
evidence: Trigger: Dashboard starts with no password hash file at ~/.hermes/.dashboard_password
Step 1: Attacker sends POST /api/login with password='attacker_password'
Step 2: handle_login() checks if password_hash_path exists (line 134) — it doesn't
Step 3: Code enters the else branch (line 140) and writes the attacker's password hash
Step 4: Attacker receives a valid session cookie
Step 5: Legitimate user tries to login with their intended password — rejected (line 137)
Outcome: Attacker has permanent admin access. Password can only be changed by manually deleting the hash file.
No rate limiting on login attempts (line 120-149) — unlimited brute force is possible
Password uses plain SHA-256 without salt (line 143) — vulnerable to rainbow table attacks
findings.suggested_fix: Pre-generate the password hash during installation/setup, not on first login. Or require a setup token/CLI command to set the initial password. Add rate limiting to the login endpoint. Use a proper password hashing algorithm (bcrypt, argon2) with salt.

findings.title: Abuse case: Revolt adapter has no user allowlist despite documented env vars — any user can interact with the bot
findings.why_it_matters: The adapter documentation references REVOLT_ALLOWED_USERS and REVOLT_ALLOW_ALL_USERS environment variables, but the code never checks them. Any Revolt user can send messages to the bot, triggering Zeus profile calls, consuming LLM API credits, and potentially accessing shared knowledge.
evidence: Trigger: Any Revolt user sends a message to a channel where the bot is present
Step 1: _on_revolt_event() receives the Message event (line 219)
Step 2: _on_message() processes the message (line 226)
Step 3: Only check is whether the author is the bot itself (line 233-235)
Step 4: No check against REVOLT_ALLOWED_USERS allowlist
Step 5: Message is dispatched to handle_message() → routes to Zeus
Outcome: Any user can trigger LLM calls, consume API credits, write/read shared knowledge
The env vars are documented in the module docstring (lines 29-30) but never implemented
REVOLT_ALLOW_ALL_USERS is also documented but not implemented
findings.suggested_fix: Implement user allowlist checking in _on_message(). Parse REVOLT_ALLOWED_USERS as a comma-separated set of user IDs. Reject messages from unauthorized users before dispatching to handle_message().

findings.title: Cascade: Dashboard WebSocket has no auth, no connection limit, and no rate limiting — open to resource exhaustion
findings.why_it_matters: The /ws endpoint bypasses auth_middleware (it's a GET, not covered by the middleware's path checks). Any client can open unlimited WebSocket connections. Each connection is stored in memory. An attacker can exhaust server memory by opening thousands of connections, and broadcast() will attempt to send to all of them.
evidence: Trigger: Attacker opens many WebSocket connections to /ws
Step 1: handle_websocket() at line 72 has no authentication check
Step 2: auth_middleware only checks request.path for /api/login and /api/health HEAD — /ws is not exempted but also not protected
Step 3: Each connection is added to WebSocketHub._connections (line 30)
Step 4: No maximum connection limit is enforced
Step 5: When broadcast() is called, it iterates over ALL connections (line 45)
Step 6: With N connections, broadcast does N send_str() calls — O(N) per broadcast
Outcome: Memory exhaustion from connection objects. CPU exhaustion from broadcast iteration. Potential DoS.
The heartbeat=30 helps clean up dead connections but doesn't prevent the initial flood
findings.suggested_fix: Add authentication to the WebSocket endpoint (check session cookie in handle_websocket). Add a maximum connection limit (e.g., 100). Add per-IP rate limiting for new connections.

findings.title: Composition failure: Dashboard API uses hardcoded DB path while share_knowledge uses configurable path — data inconsistency
findings.why_it_matters: Dashboard API reads from ~/.hermes/olympus.db (hardcoded). share_knowledge/tools.py reads from OLYMPUS_DB_PATH env var (configurable, defaulting to ~/.hermes/olympus.db). If OLYMPUS_DB_PATH is set to a different path, the dashboard shows stale/empty data while share_knowledge writes to a different database. Users see inconsistent state.
evidence: Trigger: User sets OLYMPUS_DB_PATH=/tmp/test_olympus.db
Step 1: share_knowledge writes knowledge facts to /tmp/test_olympus.db
Step 2: Dashboard API reads from ~/.hermes/olympus.db (hardcoded at line 24)
Step 3: Dashboard shows empty results — facts written by share_knowledge are invisible
Step 4: Dashboard GraphQL also uses the same hardcoded path (via get_db from api.py)
Outcome: Data split across two databases. Dashboard shows stale data. Knowledge sharing appears broken.
The seed_data.py also uses the hardcoded path (line 14), compounding the inconsistency
findings.suggested_fix: Use the same _resolve_db_path() function from share_knowledge/tools.py in dashboard/api.py. Or define a single shared DB_PATH constant in a common module that all plugins import.

findings.title: Abuse case: Dashboard GraphQL field detection uses substring matching — false triggers from variable names
findings.why_it_matters: The GraphQL query parser checks if field names appear anywhere in the query string using `if field in query_str`. A query containing 'health' in a variable name, comment, or string value will trigger the health resolver. This causes unnecessary database queries and could leak data through unexpected field resolution.
evidence: Trigger: Client sends GraphQL query: '{ wiki(domain: "health") { fact } }'
Step 1: _execute_query() receives the query string (line 112)
Step 2: It checks 'if "health" in query_str' (line 126) — TRUE, because 'health' appears in the variable value
Step 3: HealthType.resolve() is called (line 131) — unnecessary database query
Step 4: Result includes health data that the client didn't request
Outcome: Unnecessary database load. Potential data leakage. Response includes unexpected fields.
Worse: a query like '{ wiki { fact } } # TODO: fix health endpoint' would also trigger health resolver
findings.suggested_fix: Parse the query string properly to identify requested fields. Use regex with word boundaries or a proper GraphQL query parser. At minimum, check for field names followed by '{' or whitespace patterns that indicate actual field requests.

findings.title: Cascade: Supervisor idle enforcement and health monitor race on the same profile — stop/start conflict
findings.why_it_matters: The idle enforcer (background thread, 60s interval) and health monitor (background thread, 30s interval) both operate on profile processes independently. If the idle enforcer stops a profile while the health monitor sees it as 'crashed' (because it was just stopped), the health monitor may auto-restart it — defeating the idle TTL enforcement.
evidence: Trigger: On-demand profile exceeds idle TTL
Step 1: IdleEnforcer._run() calls enforce_idle_ttl() (line 163)
Step 2: enforce_idle_ttl() calls lifecycle.stop_profile() with reason='idle timeout' (line 113)
Step 3: stop_profile() sends SIGTERM, clears PID file (lifecycle.py line 148)
Step 4: Meanwhile, HealthMonitor._run() runs its 30s check (health.py line 67)
Step 5: If the timing is right, health monitor sees the profile as 'crashed' (PID file cleared but process still dying)
Step 6: If run_mode is misconfigured or the profile was recently changed to always-on, health monitor restarts it
Outcome: Profile is immediately restarted after idle kill. Idle enforcement is defeated.
Even without run_mode conflict: the stop_profile in idle and the _check_all in health both call list_profiles() which iterates the profiles directory — concurrent file I/O on PID files
findings.suggested_fix: Add a 'recently_stopped' tracking mechanism. When idle enforcer stops a profile, record the timestamp. Health monitor should skip profiles stopped within the last N seconds. Or use a shared state/lock between the two background threads.

findings.title: Resource exhaustion: Zeus routing polls all 8 specialist profiles sequentially with 10s timeout each — 80s worst-case blocking
findings.why_it_matters: When all_profiles=True, routing calls _call_profile() for each of 8 specialist profiles sequentially. Each call has a 10-second timeout. If all 8 profiles are slow or unresponsive, the call blocks for up to 80 seconds. This blocks the calling thread (potentially the Hermes gateway event loop), causing cascading timeouts for all other operations.
evidence: Trigger: Zeus calls routing with all_profiles=True while specialist profiles are slow/unresponsive
Step 1: handle_routing() iterates SPECIALIST_PROFILES (line 151)
Step 2: For each profile, _call_profile() calls subprocess.run with timeout=10 (line 111-116)
Step 3: If each profile times out, total wait = 8 × 10 = 80 seconds
Step 4: The calling thread is blocked for the entire duration
Step 5: If called from the Hermes gateway's event loop, all other operations are blocked
Outcome: 80-second blocking call. Gateway becomes unresponsive. Other platform adapters (Revolt, Dashboard) can't process events.
Note: chip_in.py uses asyncio.gather for parallel execution, but routing.py does sequential calls
findings.suggested_fix: Use concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor or asyncio.gather to poll profiles in parallel. Add a total timeout for the entire routing operation (not just per-profile). Consider a shorter default timeout for routing polls since they only need a brief assessment.

findings.title: State corruption: Supervisor idle state file loses updates under concurrent activity recording
findings.why_it_matters: record_activity() loads the entire state file, modifies one entry, and writes it back. If two activities are recorded concurrently (e.g., two tool calls to the same profile), the second write overwrites the first. The idle timer for one profile is lost, causing premature idle kills.
evidence: Trigger: Two concurrent calls to record_activity('zeus') and record_activity('chronos')
Step 1: Thread A calls record_activity('zeus') — loads state file (line 48)
Step 2: Thread B calls record_activity('chronos') — loads state file (line 48) — same snapshot as A
Step 3: Thread A updates state['zeus'] and writes (line 49-50)
Step 4: Thread B updates state['chronos'] and writes (line 49-50) — overwrites A's zeus update
Outcome: Zeus's last_activity timestamp is lost. Zeus appears idle longer than it actually is.
Consequence: Zeus gets killed by idle enforcement while actively processing requests
The _LOCK protects within a single record_activity call but not across the load-modify-save cycle when called from different processes
findings.suggested_fix: Use file locking (fcntl.flock) around the entire load-modify-save cycle. Or use SQLite for idle state instead of JSON file. Or use atomic per-profile state files instead of a single shared file.

findings.title: Timing attack: Dashboard API SQLite connections have no timeout — concurrent requests cause 'database is locked' errors
findings.why_it_matters: Each API endpoint opens a new SQLite connection without a timeout parameter. Under concurrent load (multiple dashboard tabs, GraphQL + REST + WebSocket), SQLite's file-level locking causes 'database is locked' errors. The code catches sqlite3.Error and returns 500, but doesn't retry. Users see intermittent failures.
evidence: Trigger: Multiple concurrent requests to dashboard API endpoints
Step 1: Request A opens SQLite connection (api.py line 43), starts a query
Step 2: Request B opens SQLite connection, tries to query the same database
Step 3: SQLite's default locking mode causes Request B to get 'database is locked'
Step 4: Request B's query raises sqlite3.Error, caught at line 82/119/etc.
Step 5: Request B returns 500 error to client
Outcome: Intermittent 500 errors under concurrent load. No retry logic. Users see broken dashboard.
WAL mode (used in share_knowledge and seed_data) helps but is not enabled in api.py's get_db()
No timeout parameter on sqlite3.connect() — defaults to 5 seconds, which may not be enough under load
findings.suggested_fix: Add timeout parameter to sqlite3.connect(): sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH, timeout=30). Enable WAL mode: conn.execute('PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL'). Consider connection pooling or a read-only connection for read-only endpoints.

findings.title: Abuse case: Revolt send_message retries once on rate limit but the retry can also be rate limited — unbounded retry loop
findings.why_it_matters: When rate limited (HTTP 429), send_message sleeps for retry_after seconds and then recursively calls itself. If the retry also gets rate limited, it sleeps again and retries. This creates a potential infinite retry loop that blocks the calling coroutine indefinitely.
evidence: Trigger: Revolt API returns 429 (rate limited) on send_message
Step 1: client.send_message() receives 429 response (line 105)
Step 2: Parses retry_after header, sleeps (line 107-108)
Step 3: Recursively calls self.send_message() (line 110)
Step 4: If the retry also gets 429, steps 1-3 repeat
Step 5: No max retry count — infinite loop possible
Outcome: Coroutine blocks indefinitely. No message is sent. Caller never gets a response.
The recursive call also means stack grows with each retry — potential stack overflow on persistent rate limiting
findings.suggested_fix: Add a max_retries parameter (default 1 or 2). Convert recursive call to iterative loop. Return None after max retries exceeded, letting the caller handle the failure.

findings.title: Composition failure: Dashboard auth middleware doesn't protect GraphQL endpoint — unauthenticated data access
findings.why_it_matters: The auth_middleware is registered as an aiohttp middleware on the app. However, the GraphQL route is registered separately via register_graphql_route(). If the middleware is not properly applied to all routes (e.g., if the GraphQL route is registered before the middleware is configured, or if aiohttp's middleware doesn't apply to all route types), the GraphQL endpoint could be accessed without authentication.
evidence: Trigger: Client sends POST /api/graphql without a session cookie
Step 1: auth_middleware checks request.path (auth.py line 87)
Step 2: /api/graphql is not /api/login or /api/health HEAD — should require auth
Step 3: However, the middleware is applied via web.Application(middlewares=[auth_middleware]) (dashboard/__init__.py line 45)
Step 4: aiohttp middlewares apply to all routes by default, BUT the GraphQL handler also accepts GET requests (graphql.py line 182)
Step 5: A GET request to /api/graphql with query parameters could bypass POST-specific auth checks
Outcome: Potential unauthenticated data access via GraphQL GET requests
The real risk depends on aiohttp's middleware ordering and whether the GraphQL route is properly covered
findings.suggested_fix: Verify that aiohttp middleware applies to all routes including GraphQL. Add explicit auth check in handle_graphql() as a defense-in-depth measure. Remove GET support for GraphQL if not needed (line 182).

findings.title: Cascade: Zeus routing keyword matching produces false domain matches — wrong specialist profile receives sensitive queries
findings.why_it_matters: Domain detection uses simple substring matching: `if keyword in query_lower`. This produces false positives: 'wealth' matches 'health' → routes to iaso. 'unfit' matches 'fitness' → routes to iaso. 'homeowner' matches 'home' → routes to hephaestus. Sensitive queries about wealth/finance get routed to the health profile, and vice versa.
evidence: Trigger: User asks 'How should I invest my wealth?'
Step 1: _detect_domain() lowercases the query (line 101)
Step 2: Iterates DOMAIN_MAP checking `if keyword in query_lower` (line 102-104)
Step 3: 'health' is found in 'wealth' → returns 'iaso' (health profile)
Step 4: Query about investments is routed to the health specialist
Outcome: Wrong specialist receives the query. User gets irrelevant response. Sensitive financial data is exposed to the wrong profile.

Other false positives: 'schedule' contains 'hed' (no), but 'healthcare' contains 'health' → correct. 'fitness center' contains 'fitness' → correct. 'unfit for duty' contains 'fit' → no match for 'fitness'. But 'wealth management' → 'health' match → wrong profile.
findings.suggested_fix: Use word-boundary matching (regex \bkeyword\b) instead of substring matching. Or use a proper NLP classifier. At minimum, sort keywords by length (longest first) to prefer more specific matches.

findings.title: Resource exhaustion: Zeus chip_in spawns 8 subprocesses simultaneously — OOM risk on resource-constrained systems
findings.why_it_matters: chip_in polls all 8 specialist profiles in parallel using asyncio.gather. Each profile spawns a subprocess running 'hermes -p <profile> -z <prompt>'. On a resource-constrained system (e.g., a small VPS), 8 simultaneous LLM inference processes can exhaust memory, causing OOM kills of the Hermes process itself.
evidence: Trigger: Zeus calls chip_in after responding to a user message
Step 1: handle_chip_in() creates 8 async tasks (line 114-117)
Step 2: asyncio.gather() runs all 8 tasks concurrently (line 118)
Step 3: Each task spawns a subprocess via subprocess.run (line 71-76)
Step 4: 8 hermes processes run simultaneously, each loading an LLM model
Step 5: On a system with limited RAM (e.g., 4GB), 8 LLM processes exceed available memory
Step 6: OOM killer terminates the Hermes process or individual hermes subprocesses
Outcome: Hermes crashes. All platform connections drop. User loses access.
No concurrency limit, no memory check, no graceful degradation
findings.suggested_fix: Add a concurrency limit (e.g., semaphore with max 3 concurrent subprocesses). Or poll profiles sequentially with a total timeout. Check available memory before spawning subprocesses.

findings.title: Timing attack: Supervisor stop_profile blocks for up to 10 seconds — gateway event loop stall
findings.why_it_matters: stop_profile() uses time.sleep(0.5) in a loop of 20 iterations (line 137-140), blocking for up to 10 seconds while waiting for the process to terminate. If called from the Hermes gateway's event loop (via a tool call), this blocks all other operations for 10 seconds. Revolt messages queue up, dashboard requests timeout, other tool calls stall.
evidence: Trigger: Zeus calls stop_profile('chronos') via the supervisor tool
Step 1: stop_profile() sends SIGTERM (lifecycle.py line 132)
Step 2: Enters loop: for _ in range(20): time.sleep(0.5) (line 137-140)
Step 3: If the process doesn't terminate quickly, the loop runs for 10 seconds
Step 4: time.sleep() is a blocking call — if called from the event loop thread, it blocks everything
Step 5: During these 10 seconds: Revolt WebSocket events queue, dashboard requests timeout, other tool calls stall
Outcome: 10-second gateway stall. Cascading timeouts across all platform adapters.
The tool handler _handle_stop_profile (supervisor/__init__.py line 98) calls this synchronously
findings.suggested_fix: Make stop_profile async and use asyncio.sleep() instead of time.sleep(). Or run the blocking portion in a thread pool executor. Or reduce the wait time and use a non-blocking poll mechanism.

findings.title: State corruption: Dashboard seed_data.py uses INSERT OR REPLACE — silently overwrites production data
findings.why_it_matters: seed_data.py uses INSERT OR REPLACE for all tables. If run against a production database (e.g., by accident, or by a confused admin), it silently overwrites existing agent_profiles, knowledge entries, calendar events, contacts, and preferences with test data. No warning, no confirmation, no backup.
evidence: Trigger: Admin runs `python plugins/dashboard/seed_data.py` against production database
Step 1: seed_all() connects to ~/.hermes/olympus.db (line 186)
Step 2: ensure_schema() creates tables if they don't exist (line 188)
Step 3: seed_profiles() uses INSERT OR REPLACE (line 96) — overwrites all existing profiles
Step 4: seed_knowledge() uses INSERT OR REPLACE (line 119) — overwrites all existing knowledge
Step 5: seed_calendar(), seed_contacts(), seed_preferences() all use INSERT OR REPLACE
Outcome: All production data replaced with test data. No backup. No warning.
The script has no --dry-run flag, no confirmation prompt, no environment check
findings.suggested_fix: Add a --force flag and require explicit confirmation before running against an existing database. Check if the database already has data and warn before overwriting. Use INSERT OR IGNORE instead of INSERT OR REPLACE for seed data.

residual_risks: Dashboard session secret (_SECRET) is generated once at module import and never rotated. If the secret file is compromised, all active sessions are compromised until manual file deletion and restart.
Dashboard password uses unsalted SHA-256. While this is a local-only system, rainbow table attacks are trivial for common passwords. No password complexity requirements.
Revolt bot token is stored in environment variables and config.yaml. If the config.yaml is committed to version control or the environment is leaked, the bot token is compromised.

Supervisor PID files can be spoofed. An attacker who can write to ~/.hermes/supervisor/pids/ could create a fake PID file pointing to an arbitrary process, causing stop_profile to send SIGTERM/SIGKILL to that process.

share_knowledge scope enforcement depends on scopes.json being present and correct. If the file is missing, _check_scope returns an error denying all access — but if the file is malformed, the behavior is undefined.
Zeus routing's SPECIALIST_PROMPT and CHIP_IN_PROMPT are hardcoded. If a specialist profile's behavior changes (e.g., different JSON format), the parsing silently fails and returns score 0.0.
Dashboard WebSocket broadcasts are fire-and-forget. If a broadcast fails mid-iteration (e.g., network error to one client), subsequent clients in the iteration may not receive the event.

The health monitor uses threading.Thread (not asyncio), which means it runs in a separate OS thread. If the Hermes gateway uses asyncio exclusively, the thread's subprocess calls could interact unpredictably with the event loop.
testing_gaps: No test for Revolt client session lifecycle — the authenticate() context manager bug would be caught by a simple integration test that calls send_message after authenticate().
No test for Zeus chip_in called from an async context — the asyncio.run() RuntimeError would be caught by a test that runs handle_chip_in inside an asyncio event loop.
No test for concurrent start_profile calls — the TOCTOU race condition requires a concurrent test with two threads calling start_profile simultaneously.
No test for RevoltErrorHandler retry counter exhaustion — a test that simulates 5+ consecutive errors would reveal the permanent disconnection bug.
No test for Dashboard WebSocket authentication bypass — a test that connects to /ws without a session cookie would reveal the missing auth.
No test for idle state file concurrent writes — a test with two threads calling record_activity simultaneously would reveal the lost-update bug.
No test for Supervisor health monitor restart loop — a test that simulates a profile that crashes immediately after starting would reveal the infinite restart loop.
No test for GraphQL field detection false positives — a test with 'health' in a variable name would reveal the substring matching bug.
No test for Revolt user allowlist — since the allowlist is documented but not implemented, no test exists for it (because the feature doesn't exist).
No test for Dashboard API under concurrent load — a test with multiple simultaneous requests would reveal the SQLite locking issue.
No test for Zeus routing keyword false positives — a test with queries like 'wealth management' would reveal the substring matching bug.
No test for seed_data.py safety — no test verifies that seed_data.py doesn't overwrite existing data, or that it requires confirmation.
